definition.text: External Event is the entry door for a message that crosses in from outside the platform -- a webhook push or a queue delivery -- as distinct from an occurrence the platform generates about itself at 1.3. This repo's own target architecture draws the internal/external line as one requirement: "An internal or external event must be able to enter the system." Its own worked reference model (composable-plan.md, tied explicitly to the same source) folds this door together with agent-to-agent messages under one 'External (system or agent)' column, not two: a push, a webhook and a partner agent all fire it the same way, rather than webhooks/queues (this card) and agent-to-agent (1.5) being separately evidenced doors.

evidence.quote: An internal or external event must be able to enter the system.
a push, a webhook, a partner agent

standards.role: For this door specifically, CloudEvents' HTTP WebHook specification defines the delivery method, an authorization model to protect the delivery target, and a registration handshake so the sender cannot be abused for flooding arbitrary sites -- the delivery-and-abuse-protection half that an internal event (1.3) does not need.
standards.covers: Governs HTTP-delivered webhooks only; it says nothing about queue-based delivery (broker/consumer pull, e.g. Kafka/SQS-style), which this card's own subtitle ('Webhooks / queues') also names. It also carries no internal/external attribute of its own -- the trust boundary is drawn by this repo's target architecture (T-t1-03), not by CloudEvents.

evidence.text: CloudEvents' HTTP WebHook spec defines the delivery method, an authorization model, and a registration handshake against abuse.

evidence.quote: The specification defines a HTTP method by how notifications are delivered by the sender, an authorization model for event delivery to protect the delivery target, and a registration handshake that protects the sender from being abused for flooding arbitrary HTTP sites with requests.

standards.role: Governs how a duplicate delivery of the same external event is recognised on the wire -- the mechanism at-least-once, retry-until-acked webhook delivery specifically needs.
standards.covers: Is a wire-level draft for keying a request, not a dedup implementation; it does not say what a receiver must do when a key repeats (that is cap-idempotency's own claim/lease contract), and it remains a draft, not a ratified standard.

evidence.text: The Idempotency-Key draft makes key uniqueness normative: the same key must not be reused for a different payload.

evidence.quote: The idempotency key MUST be unique and MUST NOT be reused with another request with a different request payload.

tools.name: This repo's own HTTP adapter
tools.note: F-b3-08 is a Part B (target-architecture) row -- PASS.md states Part B is 'a target architecture for a greenfield build. No code carries over' -- so this names the intended adapter, not a verified running one. The harness meant to prove it, harness/work-intake/, currently fails 24 of 28 checks (`bash harness/work-intake/test.sh`), and the row does not itself say which adapter serves which door. See gaps.

evidence.text: This repo's recorded adapters for work intake today are CLI, git event, HTTP and schedule.

tools.name: GitHub Actions push-event webhook trigger
tools.note: A named, live implementation of an externally-pushed event (a repository push originated by GitHub's own servers) starting work through a declared trigger, alongside sibling schedule and manual triggers. Not used by this repo.

evidence.text: GitHub Actions exposes push, schedule and manual-dispatch as sibling trigger kinds under one declaration key.

evidence.quote: Push triggers the workflow on code pushes to the repository, while schedule triggers the workflow at specific times or intervals, and workflow_dispatch triggers the workflow manually from the Actions tab in the repository.

tools.name: n8n Trigger Node
tools.note: Names 'external event' explicitly as one of the two things a trigger node listens for. Not used by this repo.

evidence.text: An n8n Trigger Node is the workflow entry point that listens for a specific external event or a predefined schedule.

evidence.quote: A n8n Trigger Node is the entry point of an n8n workflow that listens for a specific external event or a predefined schedule.

tools.name: Kafka / RabbitMQ (message queues)
tools.note: The two message-queue technologies this repo's own research corpus names for asynchronous event delivery -- the 'queues' half of this card's subtitle. The cited record's substance is about carrying correlation metadata through queue headers rather than the queue products themselves. Not used by this repo; no queue consumer is recorded anywhere in the corpus.

evidence.text: Producers carrying events through Kafka or RabbitMQ are expected to inject context into message metadata rather than the payload.

evidence.quote: Producers must inject a serialized context into message metadata, and consumers must extract it before creating processing spans.

landscape.text: The real tradeoff among external-event implementations is not the envelope format (CloudEvents standardises that) but delivery guarantee and who owns deduplication: webhooks are inherently at-least-once -- 'exactly-once delivery is a proven impossibility in distributed computing, not a feature any vendor can ship' -- so the receiver, not the sender, owns deduplication, and a dedup cache must outlive the sender's full retry window. Before a common envelope, that dedup burden was compounded by format fragmentation across providers: teams consuming several webhook sources faced 'five different parsers, five different signature verification schemes, and five different retry semantics embedded in payload fields.' CloudEvents collapses the parsing-and-identity half of that (id/source as a shared dedup key), but per the evidence found it does not by itself collapse the signature-verification half -- no single convention for verifying who actually sent the webhook was found anywhere in the corpus, and queue-based delivery (the other half of this card's subtitle) has its own, entirely separate broker-ACL authentication story that the webhook evidence does not address at all.

evidence.quote: Exactly-once delivery is a proven impossibility in distributed computing, not a feature any vendor can ship.
five different parsers, five different signature verification schemes, and five different retry semantics embedded in payload fields.

usage.text: A producer submits by pushing over HTTP (a webhook) or via a queue. For the push case, CloudEvents' HTTP WebHook binding is the specification found, defining the delivery method plus 'an authorization model for event delivery to protect the delivery target, and a registration handshake that protects the sender from being abused for flooding arbitrary HTTP sites with requests.' Because delivery is at-least-once, the same message can arrive more than once; the receiver is expected to deduplicate on the CloudEvents id/source pair -- that id field is the same stable identifier a dedup layer wants -- and hold that dedup record at least as long as the provider's full retry window, the same key-and-window shape cap-idempotency's own claim/lease contract requires. Per this repo's own worked reference model, whichever party submits this way is authenticated as 'the external party' and runs under 'a pre-authorised ceiling per source' rather than a budget it can set itself.

evidence.quote: The specification defines a HTTP method by how notifications are delivered by the sender, an authorization model for event delivery to protect the delivery target, and a registration handshake that protects the sender from being abused for flooding arbitrary HTTP sites with requests.
Your deduplication cache must persist at least as long as the provider's full retry window.

gaps.what: Reference-model.json splits 'External Event' (1.4, webhooks/queues) from 'Agent-to-Agent' (1.5) as two separate cards, but every primary source found treats them as one bucket: T-t6-02 says 'an external system or agent' as a single phrase, and composable-plan.md's four-doors table (explicitly mapped from the same source) gives its 'External (system or agent)' column one shared identity rule ('the external party, authenticated'), one shared budget rule ('a pre-authorised ceiling per source'), and lists 'a push, a webhook, a partner agent' together as what fires it. Nowhere in the corpus is a webhook/queue delivery shown needing different identity, budget or gate handling than an agent-to-agent message.
gaps.why_it_matters: This is the clearest evidence in the corpus that the 1.4/1.5 split is this repo's own bucketing layered on the reference model, not a distinction the source documents draw themselves. If the two doors genuinely share identity, budget and gate handling, splitting them into two cards risks documenting one seam as two.
gaps.research_query: does any part of this repo's build (schema, adapter, conformance fixture) give webhooks/queues and agent-to-agent messages different handling, or do they share one kind=external value throughout with no further field distinguishing them

gaps.what: This repo's only worked instance of kind=external (examples/end-to-end/entries/external.json) is an agent-to-agent submission ('Partner agent submits a fault it found while running its own checks'), not a webhook or queue delivery. No fixture, adapter, or example in the searched corpus shows an actual externally-pushed webhook or queue message reaching intake.
gaps.why_it_matters: The card's own subtitle names 'Webhooks / queues' specifically, and its 'built' status asserts a working door for that traffic. The evidence found supports an external-producer door generally (via agent-to-agent) but demonstrates nothing for webhooks or queues in particular.
gaps.research_query: is there a worked fixture or adapter for a webhook- or queue-delivered event, distinct from the agent-to-agent fixture already on file

gaps.what: No record in the searched corpus specifies a concrete signature-verification mechanism (header name, algorithm, key rotation) for authenticating an inbound webhook before intake accepts it. CloudEvents' own webhook binding states only that 'an authorization model' exists to protect the delivery target, without saying what it concretely requires, and the wider landscape evidence says signature schemes are exactly the thing that still differs per provider.
gaps.why_it_matters: Authentication on the way in is one of the two concrete mechanisms this card was asked to establish (the other being dedup, which is better evidenced via CloudEvents id/source). Without a named scheme, the card's built status for authentication specifically is asserted, not shown.
gaps.research_query: what signature or authorization scheme does this repo's own HTTP adapter require of an inbound webhook, if any

gaps.what: The card's subtitle bundles two transports -- webhooks (push over HTTP) and queues (pull/subscribe from a broker) -- as if they share one trust story. Nearly all evidence found is HTTP/webhook-specific (CloudEvents' WebHook binding, signature-verification fragmentation); queue-based delivery has a distinct authentication primitive (broker ACLs, SASL/mTLS) that none of the corpus records address.
gaps.why_it_matters: A push carrying a signature header and a pull authenticated by broker credentials are different mechanisms end to end; treating them as one door without evidence for the queue half means half of what 'built' claims here is simply unaddressed.
gaps.research_query: does any record distinguish queue-consumer authentication from webhook signature verification, or does this card conflate two transports with only one evidenced

gaps.what: The harness meant to prove this capability's adapter swap, harness/work-intake/, currently fails: `bash harness/work-intake/test.sh` reports 'passed 4, failed 24' -- conformance does not reach 15/15, the swap proof between adapters fails, the deliberate-breakage case does not isolate to one adapter, and the product-name scan fails. `tools/final_acceptance.py` records the same finding at the stack level: stick T-t9-06 ('every harness executes one adapter swap with its gate green') holds 'no', naming work-intake as one of three red harnesses out of 28. This door and 1.3 sit on the same failing harness and the same fixture set (examples/end-to-end/entries/*.json).
gaps.why_it_matters: This is stronger and more direct than an absence-of-evidence gap: it is a measured, machine-checked failure of the gate this repo itself wrote to prove the capability works, directly contradicting this card's 'built' status.
gaps.research_query: what specifically fails in harness/work-intake/conformance.py, and does fixing it change either the 1.3 or 1.4 card's evidence

gaps.what: The canonical entry envelope (cap-work-intake's EntryEnvelope) has one `kind` enum -- human, event, schedule, external -- and ten properties total, none of which is a trust or origin marker. The schema's own description of `kind` says it is 'recorded for audit and routing; nothing downstream of intake branches on it.' Nothing in the shape distinguishes an authenticated external party from an internal one once either is normalised into kind=event or kind=external.
gaps.why_it_matters: The owner's stated intent for the internal/external split is one envelope with a trust field. The evidence supports the 'one envelope' half but not the 'trust field' half: there is no field to audit or police the internal/external boundary post-intake, which is exactly the boundary this card and 1.3 exist to name.
gaps.research_query: should the entry envelope carry an explicit trust/origin attribute distinct from kind, and if so what would read it downstream
